answer: I'd like to talk about learning to drive, which tested my patience more than almost anything else. A time I had to keep pushing through real difficulty was while learning to drive about two years ago, which I found far harder than I had expected. I wanted to learn because my father had recently retired and was no longer comfortable driving long distances, so someone in the family needed to take the car to the village. The roads here are full of rickshaws, buses and people crossing without warning, so even a short drive felt stressful. I struggled with confidence behind the wheel and failed my first test, which was genuinely [[disheartening]]. Part of me was tempted to give up entirely and rely on buses and rickshaws instead. However, I knew driving would be a valuable skill, so I forced myself to [[persevere]]. I booked more lessons, practised early in the mornings when the roads were quiet and slowly [[chipped away at]] my nervousness. Progress was frustratingly slow at times, and it required a lot of [[patience]]. When I finally passed on my second attempt, the sense of accomplishment was immense, precisely because it had not come easily. Honestly, that experience taught me the value of [[persistence]] more than almost anything else. It proved that giving up at the first setback would have cost me a skill I now use regularly. My grandparents are always delighted when I drive my parents to visit them, and I have carried that lesson into other challenges ever since.

followUps.answer: On quiet roads, yes, especially the drive to my grandparents' village, which passes through lovely green fields. In busy town traffic, though, I still find it more tiring than enjoyable.

followUps.q: Do you think it is important for young people to learn to drive?
followUps.answer: It is useful, but not essential for everyone. In big cities, public transport or ride-sharing can be easier. In smaller towns, though, being able to drive gives you a lot more independence.
